A.explanation: Charge per carrier is $q$ in $I = Anvq$, for example $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ for an electron, not $n$.

B.explanation: Number per unit area would have unit $\text{m}^{-2}$ and with $A$ would not give the total number in a length of wire.

C.explanation: In $I = Anvq$, $n$ is the number density of charge carriers with unit $\text{m}^{-3}$.

D.explanation: Current depends on number and charge of carriers, not on their total mass per unit volume.

hints: Look at the other symbols in $I = Anvq$: $A$ is cross-sectional area and $v$ is mean drift speed, so think what $n$ must supply to count the carriers.
A length $l$ of wire has volume $Al$, so the total number of free carriers in it is volume times carriers per unit volume.
Since $q$ already means charge carried per charge carrier, $n$ must be a different quantity that describes how crowded the carriers are in the material.
walkthrough: Identify the equation: $I = Anvq$, where $I$ is current, $A$ is cross-sectional area of the conductor, $v$ is mean drift speed of the carriers, and $q$ is charge on each carrier.
Consider a section of wire of length $l$. Its volume is $Al$, so if $n$ is carriers per unit volume then total carriers present is $nAl$.
In time $t$, carriers drift distance $v t$, so charge passing a point is $(nAvt)q$. Dividing by $t$ gives $I = nAvq$, which matches the given form.
Therefore $n$ must have unit $\text{m}^{-3}$ and is called number density. This is option C.
